I am seventy-two years old now, and my legs and back are not what they used to be. I have farmed these fields in Quzhou for more than fifty years, and I know what the land here likes. I have about nine mu of good irrigated land, and my household is just me and my wife most of the year—my son works in Shijiazhuang and sends money home, so I do not need to chase risky crops. I will stick to the wheat-maize double cropping that everyone in our village grows, because the machines can handle the harvest and planting, the buyers come to the village gate, and I understand these two crops like the back of my hand. I will not grow cotton this year; at my age, bending down to spray insecticides twelve or fourteen times is too hard, and the labor is not worth the extra cash. For the winter wheat, I will rotary-till the field in early October and sow improved seed, because the county seed station says the improved varieties resist disease better than the old ones. I will put down about sixteen kilograms of nitrogen per mu, fourteen of phosphorus, and five of potassium, and I will irrigate four times—once at green-up, once at jointing, once at heading, and once at grain-filling. For the summer maize, I will plant hybrid seed right after the wheat harvest without tilling the soil again; that saves diesel and time, and the soil keeps its moisture. The maize needs about eleven kilograms of nitrogen per mu, three of phosphorus, three of potassium, and two irrigations—one right after sowing and one at the big trumpet stage. I will spray pesticides three or four times on each crop when I see aphids or rust, but no more than that, because chemicals cost money and I do not want to breathe too much of the fumes.
